concepts.name: Calculating formula mass
concepts.statement: You calculate the formula mass of a substance by multiplying each element’s average atomic mass by its subscript and adding the products.

concepts.name: Molecular mass versus formula mass
concepts.statement: For a covalent substance the formula describes one molecule, so its formula mass may be called a molecular mass; an ionic compound has no discrete molecule, so its formula mass may not. The masses of neutral atoms are used for ions as well, since the mass of an electron is negligible beside that of an atom.

concepts.name: Mole
concepts.statement: The mole is an amount unit like a pair or a dozen, and it links an easily measured property, bulk mass, to a fundamental one, the number of atoms or molecules. Chemists count particles they cannot see by weighing them, and the mole is the unit that makes that possible.

concepts.name: Avogadro’s number
concepts.statement: One mole of any substance contains the same number of entities, 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup>, so the number of atoms or molecules in a sample follows from its amount in moles. The size of the number is what lets a drop of water hold more molecules than can be clearly imagined.

concepts.name: Molar mass
concepts.statement: The molar mass of a substance is the mass in grams of 1 mole of it, and it is numerically equal to the formula mass in amu, because the atomic mass unit and the mole are defined from the same reference, carbon-12. That equality turns a formula mass read from the periodic table into a conversion factor between grams and moles.

concepts.name: Converting between mass and moles
concepts.statement: Dividing a mass by the molar mass gives the amount in moles, and multiplying an amount by the molar mass gives the mass. This is the conversion the rest of the book leans on whenever a quantity weighed on a balance must become a count of particles or the reverse.

concepts.name: Counting atoms and molecules
concepts.statement: A mass is converted to moles with the molar mass and then to a number of entities with Avogadro’s number, and the formula then gives the number of each kind of atom. The two-step chain answers questions no balance can answer directly, such as how many carbon atoms a packet of sweetener holds.

concepts.name: Formula mass
concepts.statement: The formula mass of a substance is the sum of the average masses of all the atoms represented in its chemical formula; for a covalent compound it is also the molecular mass.

concepts.name: Percent composition
concepts.statement: The percent composition of a compound is the percentage by mass of each element in it. Measuring the mass of each element is often the first step in finding an unknown compound’s formula, and the percentages are how that measurement is reported.

forms.condition: X is any one element of the compound

concepts.name: Percent composition from a formula
concepts.statement: When the formula is known, the percent composition follows from the atomic or molar masses alone, by taking one mole of the compound as the sample. This is how a fertilizer buyer compares the nitrogen in ammonia, ammonium nitrate and urea.

concepts.name: Deriving an empirical formula
concepts.statement: A formula states the relative numbers of atoms, not their masses. So convert each element’s mass to moles, divide the amounts by the smallest, and multiply by an integer if needed to reach whole numbers. The procedure turns an analysis on a balance into a chemical formula.

concepts.name: Deriving an empirical formula from percent composition
concepts.statement: When only the percentages are known, a 100-g sample is assumed, so that each element’s mass in grams is numerically its mass percentage, and the usual procedure follows.

concepts.name: Deriving a molecular formula
concepts.statement: An empirical formula gives only the relative numbers of atoms. Dividing the molecular or molar mass by the empirical formula mass gives the number of formula units in each molecule, and multiplying every subscript by that number gives the molecular formula.

forms.latex: \frac{\text{molecular or molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}=n\;\text{formula units/molecule}
forms.condition: both masses in amu, or both in g/mol
a compound whose empirical formula is A<sub>x</sub>B<sub>y</sub>, with n empirical formula units in each molecule

concepts.name: Empirical formula mass
concepts.statement: The empirical formula mass of a compound is the sum of the average atomic masses of all the atoms its empirical formula represents.

concepts.name: Solution components
concepts.statement: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, and it usually has one component, the solvent, present at a much greater concentration than the others, the solutes, which are dissolved in it. A solution in water is an aqueous solution, the kind this book meets most often.

concepts.name: Concentration
concepts.statement: The relative amount of a given component of a solution is its concentration, and the properties of a mixture depend on it, as the sweetness of a coffee depends on its sugar. A solution is called dilute or concentrated in words before any unit puts a number on it.

concepts.name: Molarity
concepts.statement: Molarity is the number of moles of solute in exactly 1 liter of solution, and it is the concentration unit of most of chemistry. The liter is of the whole solution, not of the solvent that was added.

forms.condition: the volume is that of the whole solution, not of the solvent
the molarity of a solution, written in millimoles and milliliters to shorten a titration calculation

concepts.name: Calculating with molarity
concepts.statement: The definition of molarity links three quantities, so any one of the amount of solute, the volume of solution and the molarity follows from the other two, and a molar mass brings in the mass of solute as well. Keeping a guard digit, or working the calculation in one step, keeps the rounding error out of the answer.

concepts.name: Dilution
concepts.statement: Dilution lowers the concentration of a solution by adding solvent, and it leaves the amount of solute unchanged. It is how melting ice weakens iced tea and how a laboratory prepares a working solution from a concentrated stock.

concepts.name: Dilution equation
concepts.statement: Since n = ML and the amount of solute does not change on dilution, the product of concentration and volume is the same before and after. The relation works in any units of concentration and volume that cancel, so it is written C<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = C<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.

forms.condition: a solution diluted by adding solvent; any units of concentration and volume that cancel
a solution diluted by adding solvent, so the amount of solute is unchanged

concepts.name: Solvent
concepts.statement: The solvent is the component of a solution present at a concentration higher than that of the other components.

concepts.name: Solute
concepts.statement: A solute is a component of a solution present at a concentration less than that of the solvent.

concepts.name: Aqueous solution
concepts.statement: An aqueous solution is a solution for which water is the solvent.

concepts.name: Dissolved
concepts.statement: A solute is dissolved when its components are dispersed in a solvent.

concepts.name: Concentrated
concepts.statement: A concentrated solution is one containing solute at a relatively high concentration; the term is qualitative.

concepts.name: Dilute
concepts.statement: A dilute solution is one containing solute at a relatively low concentration; the term is qualitative.

concepts.name: Mass percentage
concepts.statement: The mass percentage of a component is the ratio of its mass to the mass of the solution, expressed as a percentage. It is the unit on the labels of consumer products, and it needs only that both masses be in the same unit.

forms.condition: both masses in the same unit

concepts.name: Volume percentage
concepts.statement: A liquid dissolved in a liquid is conveniently described by the ratio of the volume of solute to the volume of solution, expressed as a percentage, since liquid volumes are easily measured.

forms.condition: both volumes in the same unit

concepts.name: Mass-volume percent
concepts.statement: A mixed unit takes the mass of solute and the volume of solution, as physiological saline is 0.9 g of solute per 100 mL and blood sugar is reported in milligrams per deciliter. Such units are common in biochemical and medical settings.

concepts.name: Parts per million and parts per billion
concepts.statement: Very low concentrations are expressed as parts per million or parts per billion, the mass ratio multiplied by 10<sup>6</sup> or 10<sup>9</sup>, just as a percentage is a part per hundred. They are the units of trace contaminants in water.

concepts.name: Converting concentration units
concepts.statement: A solution’s density converts its volume to its mass, and a molar mass converts a mass of solute to moles, so a concentration given in one unit can be expressed in another, from a mass percentage to a mass of solute or to a molarity.

concepts.name: Parts per million
concepts.statement: Parts per million (ppm) is the ratio of solute-to-solution mass multiplied by 10⁶.

concepts.name: Parts per billion
concepts.statement: Parts per billion (ppb) is the ratio of solute-to-solution mass multiplied by 10⁹.
